1416460c60288c.mp3.metin: Sleep is often seen as a time when the brain simply switches off, but research suggests the opposite. During certain stages of sleep, the brain appears to replay and reorganise what we learned during the day, which makes memories more stable. This is why many researchers argue that an all-night study session may do more harm than good. That said, scientists are careful about how far the evidence goes. Most findings come from laboratory tasks, such as remembering word lists, and it is not yet clear how well they apply to complex school subjects. What we can say with reasonable confidence is that people who sleep after learning tend to remember more than those who stay awake for the same period. So, if you have to choose between an extra hour of revision and an extra hour of sleep the night before an exam, the evidence leans towards sleep.

1535898533c81a.mp3.metin: Many people assume that the more choices they have, the happier they will be. Yet several studies in consumer behaviour suggest that a large number of options can actually make decisions harder, and leave people less satisfied with what they pick. One explanation is that when we choose among dozens of similar items, we imagine all the alternatives we gave up, and this makes our final choice feel less attractive. Another is simple fatigue: deciding takes effort, and the effort adds up. Not every study finds this effect. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that choice is always bad. Researchers point out that the effect depends on the situation. People who already know what they want, or who are choosing something important, usually cope well with many options. The problem appears mainly when the options are numerous, similar, and difficult to compare.
